theory.overview: Regularization techniques prevent neural networks from overfitting—memorizing training data instead of learning generalizable patterns. Large neural networks have millions of parameters and can easily overfit small datasets. Regularization adds constraints or penalties that encourage simpler solutions, improving generalization to unseen data. From L2 weight decay to Dropout's random neuron silencing, these methods are essential for training robust models.

sections.title: The Bias-Variance Tradeoff
sections.content: Model complexity affects two sources of error:

components.name: Bias
components.description: Error from oversimplified assumptions. High bias = underfitting.
components.sign: Training and validation error both high

components.name: Variance
components.description: Error from sensitivity to training data noise. High variance = overfitting.
components.sign: Training error low, validation error high

sections.goal: Find sweet spot: enough complexity to capture patterns, enough constraint to avoid memorizing noise
sections.visual: U-shaped curve: total error = bias² + variance

sections.title: L2 Regularization (Weight Decay)
sections.content: Add penalty proportional to squared magnitude of weights. Penalizes large weights, favoring distributed representations.
sections.effect: Shrinks weights toward zero without making them exactly zero. Also called Ridge regularization or weight decay.
sections.intuition: Many small weights are more robust than few large weights—less sensitive to input variations
sections.lambdaEffect: λ controls strength: 0 = no regularization, large λ = strong pressure toward small weights

sections.title: L1 Regularization (Lasso)
sections.content: Add penalty proportional to absolute value of weights. Tends to produce sparse solutions.
sections.effect: Drives many weights to exactly zero, performing feature selection automatically.
sections.comparison: L2 = shrink all weights. L1 = eliminate some weights entirely.
sections.geometry: L1 constraint is diamond-shaped (vertices on axes = sparsity), L2 is spherical

sections.title: Dropout
sections.content: Randomly set a fraction of neurons to zero during training. Forces network to not rely on any single neuron.
mechanism: Each training iteration: randomly drop neurons with probability p
Remaining neurons scaled by 1/(1-p) to maintain expected values
At test time: use all neurons (no dropout), scaled appropriately
sections.analogy: Like training an ensemble of sub-networks that share parameters
sections.interpretation: Prevents co-adaptation—neurons can't rely on specific other neurons being present

sections.title: Dropout Variants
sections.content: Extensions of dropout for different scenarios:

variants.name: Monte Carlo Dropout
variants.method: Keep dropout on at test time, run multiple forward passes

sections.title: Early Stopping
sections.content: Monitor validation loss during training. Stop when validation loss stops improving, even if training loss continues decreasing.
procedure: Track validation loss every N epochs
Save model checkpoint when validation loss improves
Stop if no improvement for patience epochs
sections.benefit: Simple, effective, prevents overtraining without modifying loss function

sections.title: Data Augmentation
sections.content: Artificially expand training data by applying transformations that preserve labels.
sections.effect: Increases effective dataset size, improves robustness to input variations
sections.rule: Only apply transformations that don't change the label (e.g., rotating 6 vs 9 changes label!)

keyConcepts.name: Overfitting
keyConcepts.description: Model memorizes training data including noise, performs poorly on new data.

keyConcepts.name: Co-adaptation
keyConcepts.description: Neurons become dependent on specific other neurons, losing robustness.
keyConcepts.prevention: Dropout forces neurons to work with random subsets of partners
keyConcepts.result: Each neuron must be useful on its own

keyConcepts.name: Ensemble Interpretation
keyConcepts.description: Dropout at test time with scaling is approximately averaging predictions from exponentially many thinned networks.
keyConcepts.benefit: Ensemble methods typically outperform single models
keyConcepts.cost: Dropout is cheaper than training separate networks

keyConcepts.name: Effective Capacity
keyConcepts.description: Regularization reduces model's effective capacity without changing architecture.
keyConcepts.analogy: Like having 1000 employees but randomly sending 500 home each day—you learn to operate with reduced staff

complexity.l2: $O(n)$ per update where n = number of weights—minimal overhead
complexity.dataAug: Depends on transformation. Geometric: fast. Complex synthesis: expensive.

steps.title: Validation Check
steps.latex: \text{if } L_{val} \text{ not improved for } P \text{ epochs: stop}$

steps.title: Test-Time Scaling
steps.description: Use all neurons at test time.

practiceProblems.title: L2 vs L1 Effect
practiceProblems.description: You have weights [0.5, 2.0, -0.1, 0.0] and λ=0.1. What's the L2 penalty? L1 penalty?
practiceProblems.explanation: L2 penalizes large weights more heavily (quadratic). L1 treats all non-zero weights linearly. L1 will drive small weights to exactly zero; L2 keeps them small but non-zero.

practiceProblems.title: Dropout Scaling
practiceProblems.description: Dropout rate p=0.5. If a neuron has activation 2.0 during training, what's its expected activation? What should it be at test time?
practiceProblems.answer: Training: expected 1.0 (50% chance of 2, 50% of 0). At test: use all neurons, scale by 0.5 → 1.0. This maintains expected values.
practiceProblems.explanation: During training, neurons are kept with prob (1-p), so expected activation is (1-p)×a. At test, we use all neurons but multiply by (1-p) to match training distribution. Alternative: scale by 1/(1-p) during training (Inverted Dropout, more common).

practiceProblems.title: Overfitting Detection
practiceProblems.description: Your model achieves 98% training accuracy but only 75% validation accuracy. What should you do?
practiceProblems.answer: This is overfitting. Apply: (1) Dropout (0.2-0.5), (2) L2 regularization (λ=0.001-0.01), (3) Early stopping, (4) Data augmentation, (5) Simpler architecture.
practiceProblems.explanation: 23% gap indicates severe overfitting. Multiple techniques together work better than one. Start with dropout (easy, effective) and early stopping (prevents wasted training). Monitor validation curve to see improvement.

practiceProblems.title: Ensemble vs Dropout
practiceProblems.description: Why is dropout at test time (averaging predictions) better than a single forward pass without dropout?
practiceProblems.answer: It's effectively an ensemble of 2^n thinned networks (n = number of droppable neurons). Ensembles reduce variance and improve generalization.
practiceProblems.explanation: Monte Carlo dropout (running multiple forward passes with dropout enabled) approximates Bayesian inference, giving uncertainty estimates. But even simple weight scaling (standard dropout) approximates this ensemble average, providing regularization benefits without multiple inference cost.

practiceProblems.title: Regularization Strength
practiceProblems.description: How should you tune λ (regularization strength)? What happens if too large or too small?
practiceProblems.answer: Cross-validation: try log-spaced values (1e-5 to 10). Too small: no regularization effect. Too large: underfitting (weights near zero, model too simple).
practiceProblems.explanation: Typical L2 λ values: 1e-4 to 1e-2. Monitor validation loss vs λ on a log scale. You want the λ just before validation loss starts increasing (underfitting). Grid search or random search common.

practiceProblems.title: BatchNorm as Regularization
practiceProblems.description: How does Batch Normalization act as a regularizer even without explicit noise injection?
practiceProblems.answer: BatchNorm adds noise through mini-batch statistics. Each sample's normalized value depends on random batchmates, creating slight variation—similar to dropout's noise injection.
practiceProblems.explanation: The mean μ_B and variance σ²_B are random variables (functions of batch samples). This adds noise to activations, especially with small batch sizes. At test time, fixed population statistics remove this noise. Combined with dropout, can be too much regularization.

minigame.title: Regularization Lab
minigame.description: Train a neural network with different regularization techniques. Watch how L2 shrinks weights, how Dropout creates robust features, and how early stopping prevents overfitting. Visualize weight distributions and decision boundaries.
instructions: Select dataset with potential for overfitting
Choose regularization: L1, L2, Dropout, or combination

codeExample.code:
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.optim as optim

class RegularizedNet(nn.Module):
    """
    Neural network with dropout and batch norm
    """
    def __init__(self, input_size, hidden_size, num_classes, dropout_rate=0.5):
        super().__init__()
        
        self.layer1 = nn.Linear(input_size, hidden_size)
        self.bn1 = nn.BatchNorm1d(hidden_size)  # Also acts as regularizer
        self.dropout1 = nn.Dropout(dropout_rate)
        
        self.layer2 = nn.Linear(hidden_size, hidden_size)
        self.bn2 = nn.BatchNorm1d(hidden_size)
        self.dropout2 = nn.Dropout(dropout_rate)
        
        self.layer3 = nn.Linear(hidden_size, num_classes)
    
    def forward(self, x, training=True):
        # Layer 1
        x = self.layer1(x)
        x = self.bn1(x)
        x = torch.relu(x)
        x = self.dropout1(x) if training else x * 0.5  # Scale at test time
        
        # Layer 2
        x = self.layer2(x)
        x = self.bn2(x)
        x = torch.relu(x)
        x = self.dropout2(x) if training else x * 0.5
        
        # Output
        x = self.layer3(x)
        return x

def train_with_regularization(model, train_loader, val_loader, epochs=50, 
                               l2_lambda=0.001, device='cuda'):
    """
    Training with L2 regularization and early stopping
    """
    criterion = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()
    optimizer = optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=0.001, weight_decay=l2_lambda)
    
    model.to(device)
    
    best_val_loss = float('inf')
    patience = 10
    patience_counter = 0
    best_model_state = None
    
    history = {'train_loss': [], 'val_loss': [], 'train_acc': [], 'val_acc': []}
    
    for epoch in range(epochs):
        # Training
        model.train()
        train_loss = 0
        train_correct = 0
        train_total = 0
        
        for batch_idx, (data, target) in enumerate(train_loader):
            data, target = data.to(device), target.to(device)
            data = data.view(data.size(0), -1)
            
            optimizer.zero_grad()
            
            # Forward with dropout
            output = model(data, training=True)
            
            # Data loss
            loss = criterion(output, target)
            
            # L2 is handled by weight_decay in optimizer
            # But we can also add it manually for more control:
            # l2_reg = sum(p.pow(2).sum() for p in model.parameters())
            # loss += l2_lambda * l2_reg
            
            loss.backward()
            optimizer.step()
            
            train_loss += loss.item()
            _, predicted = output.max(1)
            train_total += target.size(0)
            train_correct += predicted.eq(target).sum().item()
        
        train_loss /= len(train_loader)
        train_acc = 100. * train_correct / train_total
        
        # Validation
        model.eval()
        val_loss = 0
        val_correct = 0
        val_total = 0
        
        with torch.no_grad():
            for data, target in val_loader:
                data, target = data.to(device), target.to(device)
                data = data.view(data.size(0), -1)
                
                # Forward without dropout (or with scaling)
                output = model(data, training=False)
                loss = criterion(output, target)
                
                val_loss += loss.item()
                _, predicted = output.max(1)
                val_total += target.size(0)
                val_correct += predicted.eq(target).sum().item()
        
        val_loss /= len(val_loader)
        val_acc = 100. * val_correct / val_total
        
        history['train_loss'].append(train_loss)
        history['val_loss'].append(val_loss)
        history['train_acc'].append(train_acc)
        history['val_acc'].append(val_acc)
        
        # Early stopping check
        if val_loss < best_val_loss:
            best_val_loss = val_loss
            patience_counter = 0
            best_model_state = model.state_dict().copy()
        else:
            patience_counter += 1
        
        if patience_counter >= patience:
            print(f'Early stopping at epoch {epoch}')
            break
        
        if epoch % 5 == 0:
            print(f'Epoch {epoch}: Train Acc: {train_acc:.2f}%, Val Acc: {val_acc:.2f}%')
    
    # Restore best model
    if best_model_state:
        model.load_state_dict(best_model_state)
    
    return history

def compare_regularization(train_loader, val_loader, input_size, num_classes):
    """
    Compare different regularization strategies
    """
    configs = [
        ('No Regularization', 0.0, 0.0),
        ('L2 Only (λ=0.001)', 0.001, 0.0),
        ('Dropout Only (p=0.5)', 0.0, 0.5),
        ('L2 + Dropout', 0.001, 0.5),
    ]
    
    results = []
    
    for name, l2_lambda, dropout in configs:
        print(f"\n=== {name} ===")
        
        model = RegularizedNet(input_size, 256, num_classes, dropout_rate=dropout)
        history = train_with_regularization(
            model, train_loader, val_loader, 
            epochs=50, l2_lambda=l2_lambda
        )
        
        final_val_acc = history['val_acc'][-1]
        results.append((name, final_val_acc))
        
        # Weight statistics
        total_params = sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters())
        l1_norm = sum(p.abs().sum().item() for p in model.parameters())
        l2_norm = sum(p.pow(2).sum().item() for p in model.parameters()) ** 0.5
        
        print(f'Final Val Acc: {final_val_acc:.2f}%')
        print(f'L1 norm: {l1_norm:.2f}, L2 norm: {l2_norm:.2f}')
    
    print("\n=== Summary ===")
    for name, acc in results:
        print(f'{name}: {acc:.2f}%')

# Custom regularization: DropConnect
class DropConnect(nn.Module):
    """
    Drop individual connections instead of neurons
    """
    def __init__(self, p=0.5):
        super().__init__()
        self.p = p
    
    def forward(self, weight):
        if self.training:
            mask = torch.bernoulli(torch.ones_like(weight) * (1 - self.p))
            return weight * mask / (1 - self.p)
        return weight

if __name__ == "__main__":
    print("=== Regularization Techniques ===\n")
    
    # Show weight decay effect
    weight = torch.tensor([1.0, 2.0, 0.5, 3.0])
    lambda_l2 = 0.1
    lambda_l1 = 0.1
    
    l2_penalty = lambda_l2 * (weight ** 2).sum()
    l1_penalty = lambda_l1 * weight.abs().sum()
    
    print(f'Weights: {weight}')
    print(f'L2 penalty (λ={lambda_l2}): {l2_penalty.item():.3f}')
    print(f'L1 penalty (λ={lambda_l1}): {l1_penalty.item():.3f}')
    
    # Dropout example
    print(f"\n=== Dropout Example ===")
    dropout = nn.Dropout(p=0.5)
    x = torch.ones(10)
    
    print(f'Input: {x}')
    dropout.train()
    dropped = dropout(x)
    print(f'Training (50% dropped): {dropped}')
    print(f'  (Note: remaining values scaled by 2)')
    
    dropout.eval()
    eval_out = dropout(x)
    print(f'Eval (no dropout): {eval_out}')
    
    print(f"\n=== Early Stopping ===")
    print(f'Patience: 10 epochs')
    print(f'Best model restored when validation loss stops improving')
